content: Tannins are a class of astringent, bitter-tasting plant polyphenols that have the ability to bind and precipitate proteins. The term tannin originates from their historical use in the tanning of animal hides to produce leather. However, the term is now broadly applied to any large polyphenolic compound that contains sufficient hydroxyl and other functional groups, such as carboxyls, to form strong complexes with proteins and other macromolecules. Tannins typically have molecular weights ranging from 500 to over 3,000. They are generally categorized into two main types: hydrolyzable tannins and condensed tannins (also known as proanthocyanidins). Hydrolyzable Tannins Hydrolyzable tannins are characterized by a central polyol carbohydrate core, often D-glucose, whose hydroxyl groups are partially or fully esterified with phenolic acids such as gallic acid (in gallotannins) or ellagic acid (in ellagitannins). These tannins can be hydrolyzed by weak acids or bases, yielding their carbohydrate and phenolic acid components. An example of a hydrolyzable tannin is tannic acid (C76H52O46), which consists of gallic acid esters of glucose and is found in the leaves and bark of various plant species. Condensed Tannins Condensed tannins, or proanthocyanidins, are polymers composed of 2 to 50 (or more) flavonoid units linked by carbon-carbon bonds, which are resistant to hydrolysis. While most condensed tannins and hydrolyzable tannins are water-soluble, some very large condensed tannins are insoluble. Foods Containing Tannins Tea The tea plant (Camellia sinensis) is naturally rich in tannins. When tea leaves are steeped in hot water, they release a tart, astringent flavor characteristic of tannins. This flavor is primarily due to catechins and other flavonoids. Tea tannins are chemically distinct from other plant tannins, such as tannic acid, and tea extracts have been shown to contain no tannic acid. Wine Tannins, particularly condensed tannins, are also present in wine, especially red wine. These tannins can originate from various sources, including grape skins and seeds, which are more prominent in red wines due to fermentation in contact with these components. Grape-derived tannins are condensed tannins, composed of procyanidin monomers, while hydrolyzable tannins are extracted from oak barrels used for aging wine. Hydrolyzable tannins are more prone to oxidation than condensed tannins. Modern winemaking techniques aim to minimize undesirable tannins from grape seeds by gently crushing grapes to extract juice. Pressing grapes produces press wine, which is more tannic and often kept separate. Wines aged in oak or wooden casks can also acquire tannins. Tannins play a crucial role in preventing oxidation during wine aging and contribute to the sediment found in aged wines. Recent studies have shown that tannins, particularly procyanidins, have beneficial effects on vascular health by suppressing the production of peptides responsible for arterial hardening. Wines from regions like southwest France and Sardinia, which are rich in procyanidins, are associated with populations that have longer lifespans. Fruits Pomegranates Pomegranates are rich in a variety of tannins, particularly hydrolyzable tannins. The most abundant tannins in pomegranates are punicalagins, which are the primary contributors to the antioxidant and health benefits of pomegranate juice. Dietary supplements and nutritional products containing pomegranate extracts are often standardized to punicalagins, the marker compound of pomegranate. Pomegranate extracts are recognized as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) by the United States Food and Drug Administration. It is recommended to use pomegranate ingredients that mimic the natural polyphenol ratio of the fruit, as synergistic effects have been observed in natural spectrum extracts, particularly pomegranate concentrates normalized to punicalagins. Persimmons Certain persimmons, such as the Korean, American, and Hachiya (Japanese) varieties, are highly astringent and inedible unless they are extremely ripe. This is due to their high tannin content. When consumed, the tannins cause a drying sensation in the mouth, as they bind to salivary proteins, rendering the saliva ineffective against the tannin-laden food. Berries Many berries, including cranberries, strawberries, and blueberries, contain both hydrolyzable and condensed tannins. Nutritional Considerations Excessive consumption of tannins can inhibit the absorption of minerals such as iron. This occurs because tannins act as metal ion chelators, forming complexes with metal ions that are not bioavailable. However, this property may be beneficial during infections, as the immune system sequesters iron to limit microbial growth. Tannins have also been shown to precipitate proteins, which can inhibit nutrient absorption in some ruminant animals consuming high-tannin grains like sorghum. Uses of Tannins Tannins are a key component in the leather tanning process. Traditionally, oak bark has been the primary source of tannins for tanneries, although inorganic tanning agents are also used today. Medicinally, tannins are employed in antidiarrheal, hemostatic, and antihemorrhoidal formulations. Tannins produce different colors when treated with ferric chloride, ranging from blue or blue-black to greenish-black, depending on the type of tannin. Iron gall ink is made by reacting tannins with iron(II) sulfate. Tannins are also used in industrial applications, such as adhesives for particleboard, developed by organizations like the Tanzania Industrial Research and Development Organization and Forintek Labs Canada. Potential Medical Applications Tannins, including galloand ellagic acid derivatives (epigallitannins), have been identified as inhibitors of HIV replication. Compounds such as 1,3,4-tri-O-galloylquinic acid, 3,5-di-O-galloyl-shikimic acid, 3,4,5-tri-O-galloylshikimic acid, punicalin, and punicalagin have demonstrated the ability to inhibit HIV replication in infected H9 lymphocytes with minimal cytotoxicity. Additionally, punicalin and punicacortein C have been shown to inhibit purified HIV reverse transcriptase.
